svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. Who knows your address, who knows your destination, and who knows both
svg.desc: A table comparing five arrangements. With no tunnel, the network operator knows both your address and your destinations. With a single tunnel, the provider knows both. With a provider's own multi-hop, two servers each know one half but the provider operates both. With two different providers chained, each knows one half and neither knows both, which requires them to combine records to reconstruct the path. With a tunnel followed by Tor, the provider knows your address and that you use Tor, and no single party knows both ends. A band below lists what none of these arrangements changes: the account you hold, the payment that identifies you, your browser fingerprint, and everything you do while signed in.
svg.text: Figure 1: Who Knows Your Address, Who Knows Where You Went
Multi-hop splits knowledge between parties. It does not remove it, and the column that matters is the third one.
the arrangement that earns the name
The provider, plus that you use Tor
and see Figure 3 for the limit
Read the third column, not the first
Row three is sold as multi-hop and delivers a split between two machines run by one company, under one legal identity, reachable by one legal process.
Row four is a split between two companies. The difference is what the word is supposed to mean.
And three things every row of this table has in common

g.text: Your account and your payment. Whoever you bought from can connect the subscription to you unless the architecture from Lesson 6.3 prevents it. Two hops does not.
Signing in. The destination knows exactly who you are the moment you log into an account, whatever address the request arrived from.
Your browser fingerprint, and the application components from Lesson 5.2. Unchanged by every row above, because none of this happens at the network layer.

svg.text: So multi-hop answers one question well: it stops any single party holding both halves. That is a real property and a narrow one.
If your problem is anything in the red band, adding hops is the wrong tool and no number of them will help.
